strengths: Novel and well-motivated adaptation of cross-layer transcoders (CLTs), previously used for LLM circuit tracing, to protein language models—addressing a real gap where SAE-based pLM interpretability methods cannot serve as replacement models because they ignore inter-layer MLP computation.

Strong quantitative results: ProtoMech recovers 82-89% of ESM2 performance on family classification and function prediction while circuits use <1% of the latent space, and it consistently and substantially outperforms the per-layer transcoder (PLT) baseline across both tasks.

Thorough set of ablations across replacement model variants (direct, sequential, full) and architectures (CLT vs PLT), presented transparently in extensive appendices, including analyses of latent counts per layer and performance in low-ESM2-performance regimes.

Qualitative case studies (protein kinase HRD motif, NADP+/Rossmann fold binding domain, GB1 mutational sensitivity) provide biologically plausible validation that discovered circuits align with known structural/functional motifs and can be traced across layers to a coherent narrative.

Steering experiments benchmark against a reasonable contemporary baseline (Contrastive Activation Addition) and random mutation, with circuit-based steering shown to outperform CAA across all DMS assays tested and to outperform PLT circuits in the majority of cases.

Detailed, well-documented open-source visualization tool with clear description of interface components (grid view, latent rankings, sequence/alignment/influence panels, interactive canvas), supporting reproducibility and adoption by the community.
Honest and specific limitations discussion (quadratic parameter growth of CLT decoders, reliance on manual/human interpretation for annotating circuits, restriction to current biological knowledge).
weaknesses: All experiments use only the small ESM2-8M model; it is unclear whether the CLT approach scales computationally (decoder parameters grow O(L^2)) or qualitatively to larger, more practically relevant pLMs (e.g., ESM2-650M or larger), which limits the significance of the contribution.

The 'denoising' claim that ProtoMech circuits outperform the original ESM2 model is demonstrated only in regimes where ESM2 itself performs poorly (F1<0.5, Spearman<0.2), where such comparisons may be dominated by noise rather than a genuine denoising effect; no rigorous statistical test is provided to substantiate this as a meaningful phenomenon rather than an artifact of a near-random baseline.

Steering results (Table 1 and appendix Tables 3-5) show considerable variance and several near-zero or negative mean/top-k scores (e.g., GRB2_HUMAN, RASK_HUMAN_abundance), and the headline claim of outperforming PLT 'in 71% of cases' represents a fairly modest margin of superiority that is not uniformly strong across assays.

The qualitative motif analysis, while illustrative, relies on manual selection of 2-3 representative case studies rather than a systematic, quantitative motif-recovery evaluation across the full set of discovered circuits, limiting the strength of the 'recovers known biological motifs' claim.

Circuit discovery is anchored entirely to supervised downstream probes (family classification, function regression) rather than the pLM's native masked-language-modeling objective; while justified in the appendix, this design choice means the recovered circuits characterize probe behavior as much as intrinsic ESM2 computation, and it is unclear how representative these two tasks are of the broader range of properties pLMs encode.

The comparison to SAE-based approaches (Appendix G) is very brief and largely conceptual, without an empirical head-to-head comparison of circuit/motif recovery quality against a strong SAE-based interpretability baseline.

Statistical rigor is limited to standard deviations and unexplained significance stars in figures; no explicit description of the statistical tests used to support significance claims is given in the main text.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually clear extension of cross-layer transcoders (CLTs), previously developed for LLM circuit tracing, to protein language models, framing circuit discovery for ESM2 via a genuine replacement-model formulation rather than per-layer SAEs/PLTs.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical protocol: evaluates on two distinct downstream task families (protein family classification and DMS-based function prediction), compares multiple replacement-model variants (direct, sequential, full) and reports results across many DMS assays and cross-validation schemes (Tables 1, 3-5, Figs 5-8).
Steering experiments benchmark against multiple relevant baselines (PLT, Contrastive Activation Addition, random mutation), with circuits found to outperform CAA and random on most of 7 DMS assays.

Includes several interpretable, qualitatively compelling case studies (protein kinase HRD motif, NADP+/Rossmann fold binding domains, GB1 mutational sensitivity) that connect discovered latents to literature-documented structural/functional motifs, and ties mutation effects (A24W, W43Q) to plausible mechanistic narratives.
Open-sources code and a detailed interactive visualization tool (circuit canvas, latent ranking, sequence/alignment/influence panels), supporting reproducibility and further community use.
Honest limitations section acknowledging O(L^2) parameter scaling, reliance on manual interpretation for motif labeling, and lack of automated annotation pipelines.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on ESM2-8M, the smallest ESM2 variant (L=6, d_model=320). There is no evidence the approach scales to the larger ESM2 models (e.g., 150M-650M+) that are actually used in practice for structure/function prediction, which substantially limits the claimed significance for 'protein circuit tracing' broadly construed; the stated O(L^2) parameter/compute cost compounds this scalability concern without any mitigating experiments.

The replacement model is considerably lossy: even using all latents, ProtoMech recovers only 82-89% of original ESM2 performance, and discovered 'circuits' recover only 74-79%; variance is large (e.g., F1 0.82±0.19) with overlapping error bars across many comparisons (Figs 5, 7, 8), making several headline claims of outperforming PLT appear statistically fragile without formal significance testing beyond annotated asterisks in Fig. 1.

Biological-motif correspondence claims (Section 3.3, Figs 3-4) rest on a small number of hand-picked, qualitative case studies explicitly described by the authors as 'by no means exhaustive.' There is no systematic/quantitative validation (e.g., enrichment statistics over many families/motifs) that circuit latents reliably align with known biology, so the central interpretability claim is largely anecdotal.

Fitness evaluation for steering relies on a CNN surrogate trained with the same architecture/procedure used for circuit-discovery probes, raising circularity/consistency concerns; no wet-lab or orthogonal computational validation of generated high-fitness variants is provided.

The circuit discovery algorithm uses a simple gradient×activation attribution with greedy top-k inclusion; no necessity (ablation/knockout) testing is performed to confirm identified latents are causally required, only that including them is sufficient to approach performance targets.

The paper notes a somewhat unexplained and potentially concerning phenomenon where sparsified/circuit representations outperform the full ESM2 model particularly when ESM2 performs poorly; this is described post hoc as 'denoising' but is not rigorously investigated, leaving open whether the replacement model is actually capturing the original model's mechanism or diverging from it in ways that happen to help weak-performance regimes.

Comparisons are essentially limited to one baseline family (PLT) plus CAA; no comparison to other circuit-discovery or interpretability baselines (e.g., SAE-based causal tracing, attribution patching) is provided empirically, only a qualitative discussion (Appendix G).

strengths: Introduces cross-layer transcoders (CLTs) for protein language models, a well-motivated extension of recent NLP mechanistic-interpretability work (Ameisen et al., 2025) that explicitly models inter-layer computation rather than treating layers independently as in SAEs or per-layer transcoders (PLTs); this addresses a clear conceptual gap in the pLM interpretability literature.

Comprehensive quantitative evaluation across two distinct downstream tasks (protein family classification and DMS-based function prediction) with consistent, sizable improvements of ProtoMech circuits over the PLT baseline (e.g., 0.73 vs 0.49 F1 for family circuits; 0.38 vs 0.35 Spearman for function circuits), while using <1% of the latent space.

Thorough ablation of replacement-model variants (direct, sequential, full replacement) for both CLTs and PLTs, reported transparently in the appendix (Figs. 5-8, Tables 3-5), which strengthens confidence that the main comparisons are not cherry-picked.

Steering experiments benchmarked against multiple sensible baselines (PLT, Contrastive Activation Addition, random mutation) across seven DMS assays, with ProtoMech outperforming PLT in 71% of cases and clearly beating CAA/random, supporting a causal/functional (not just correlational) validation of discovered circuits.

Rich, well-illustrated qualitative case studies (protein kinase HRD motif, NADP+/FAD binding domain, GB1 mutation sensitivity) that connect discovered latents to known structural/biochemical motifs, adding interpretive credibility beyond aggregate metrics.
Release of an open-source visualization tool with detailed documentation (Appendix F, Figs. 9-14), supporting reproducibility and enabling the broader community to inspect and extend circuits.

Honest and specific limitations discussion (quadratic parameter scaling with CLTs, reliance on manual/human annotation for biological interpretation, bounded by current biological knowledge) rather than generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: All experiments use only the smallest ESM2 variant (ESM2-8M, 6 layers, d=320); it is unclear whether the method's compression ratios, circuit interpretability, and steering gains generalize to larger, more practically used pLMs (e.g., 150M-3B parameter ESM2), which limits the demonstrated significance of the contribution.

The qualitative biological-motif analysis is based on only three representative case studies, explicitly acknowledged by the authors as 'by no means exhaustive'; conclusions about ProtoMech 'recovering known biological motifs' rest on a small, manually curated sample rather than a systematic/quantitative audit.

Fitness evaluation for steering experiments relies on a CNN proxy model trained on the same (often small) DMS datasets used for circuit discovery, raising some concern about circularity/overfitting in the evaluation pipeline; there is no wet-lab or orthogonal computational validation of generated high-fitness sequences.

Many reported metrics carry large standard deviations (e.g., F1 0.82±0.19, Spearman 0.41±0.19) and the paper does not clearly specify the statistical test underlying the significance markers (*, **, ***) shown in Fig. 1, making it harder to assess robustness of the ProtoMech-vs-PLT comparisons.

CLT training incurs substantial computational overhead (~3.5x parameters of the base model, O(L^2) decoder scaling), which the paper acknowledges but does not empirically address for scaling beyond the tiny 6-layer model tested, leaving open how practical the approach is for realistically sized pLMs.

The comparison to sparse autoencoders (Appendix G) is only conceptual/schematic rather than an empirical head-to-head on the same downstream tasks, so the claimed advantage over SAE-based interpretability methods is asserted rather than directly demonstrated.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated extension of cross-layer transcoders (CLTs) — previously used for LLM circuit tracing — to protein language models, addressing a genuine gap (per-layer SAE/transcoder methods ignore cross-layer computation).

Extensive empirical validation across two model scales (ESM2-8M, ESM2-35M), two downstream task families (protein family classification and DMS-based function prediction), and multiple replacement-model variants (direct, sequential, full), with a fair PLT baseline trained under matched conditions.

Circuits are shown to be highly compressed (often <1% of latent space) while retaining a large fraction (up to ~79-85%) of full-model performance, and results are broadly consistent when scaling to ESM2-35M and using a more scalable 'windowed CLT' variant.

Steering experiments across seven DMS assays show consistent gains over CAA and random baselines, and even outperform dedicated black-box optimizers (PEX, GGS) on two assays, suggesting practical utility beyond interpretability.

Qualitative case studies (kinase domain, NADP+ binding, GB1 fitness landscape) connect discovered circuit nodes to established structural/biochemical motifs (HRD motif, G-loop, Rossmann fold, Fc-binding interface), adding some biological plausibility to the recovered circuits.

Thorough appendices covering architecture/hyperparameters, alternative replacement-model formulations, additional ablations, and an interactive visualization tool; code and visualizer are released for reproducibility.

Honest discussion of limitations, including reliance on manual annotation for circuit interpretation, quadratic parameter scaling of CLTs with depth, and the current restriction to masked (non-autoregressive) pLM architectures.
weaknesses: The biological motif case studies (Figs. 3-4) are qualitative and selective (the paper itself notes these 'are by no means exhaustive'), with no systematic, quantitative benchmark against known motif/binding-site annotations across many proteins, leaving open the risk of selective/cherry-picked examples rather than a rigorous test of biological fidelity.

Steering quality is evaluated using a CNN model trained on the same DMS data used to derive circuits and steering directions; because ProtoMech circuits are also derived from probes/attributions on this same data distribution, the evaluation may be partly circular (favoring methods aligned with the CNN's inductive biases) rather than an independent test of true fitness, and no wet-lab or orthogonal computational validation is provided.

Reconstruction/circuit fidelity is still substantially below the original model in many settings (e.g., 74-79% recovery for circuits, and even full-latent CLTs sometimes only reach 82-89% of ESM2 performance), which tempers claims that the discovered pathways are a faithful 'replacement' of the target computation.

Experiments are restricted to small pLMs (8M and 35M parameters); Table 10 shows the vanilla CLT approach is computationally infeasible at scale (very high estimated training time for 650M+ parameter models), and although 'windowed CLTs' are proposed as a remedy, they are only validated on the 35M model, leaving scalability to state-of-the-art (hundreds of millions to billions of parameters) pLMs largely unresolved.

The intriguing 'denoising' phenomenon (circuits outperforming ESM2 when ESM2 performs poorly) is reported but not rigorously disentangled from potential artifacts of probe/CNN evaluation choices, so the mechanistic interpretation offered is speculative.

Comparisons to black-box optimization baselines (PEX, GGS) are conducted on only two of the twelve DMS assays used elsewhere in the paper, limiting the generality of the claim that circuit-based steering is competitive with dedicated optimizers.
Statistical rigor is uneven: most tables report means ± standard deviations without formal significance testing, and only a subset of the headline comparisons (Fig. 1) carry significance markers.

Interpretation of circuits fundamentally depends on manual labeling against existing biological knowledge (acknowledged as a limitation), which constrains the scale and objectivity of the qualitative analysis and could mask cases where recovered latents do not correspond to genuine mechanisms.

strengths: Novel extension of cross-layer transcoders (CLTs), previously applied to LLMs, to protein language models, with a full pipeline: replacement-model training, greedy circuit discovery via gradient attribution, activation-clamping steering, and an interactive visualization tool.

Extensive ablations comparing direct/sequential/full replacement strategies and CLT vs. per-layer transcoder (PLT) baselines, with results reported across two model scales (ESM2-8M and ESM2-35M) and multiple DMS assay cross-validation schemes.

Steering experiments benchmark against multiple reasonable baselines (random mutation, CAA, PEX, GGS) and show that circuit-based steering with ProtoMech generally outperforms these alternatives on several DMS assays.

The qualitative case studies (protein kinase HRD motif, NADP+/Rossmann fold binding, GB1 hydrophobic core) provide plausible, biologically grounded narratives connecting discovered latents to known structural/functional motifs.
Reasonable engineering effort: released code, a windowed-CLT variant to address O(L^2) parameter scaling, and a visualizer tool, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The method is only demonstrated on very small pLMs (8M and 35M parameters). The paper's own scaling table (Table 10) shows that training vanilla CLTs on realistically-sized ESM2 models (650M, 3B, 15B) would require hundreds to thousands of GPU-days, and even the proposed windowed-CLT mitigation is only validated at 35M scale. This casts doubt on whether the framework is practically applicable to the large pLMs that are actually used in the field, undermining the significance of the contribution.

The qualitative biological-motif analysis (Figs. 3-4) is based on only three hand-picked case studies, and the paper explicitly states these examples were 'selected for annotation availability and representative cross-layer coverage' and are 'by no means exhaustive.' There is no systematic, quantitative validation (e.g., against a curated set of known catalytic/binding site annotations) that circuits reliably align with ground-truth biology beyond these anecdotes.

Headline recovery numbers carry large variances (e.g., F1 0.82±0.19 for family circuits, Spearman 0.41±0.19 for function circuits; PLT/CLT gaps are sometimes within one standard deviation of each other in Figs. 5/7/8), which weakens the strength of claims that ProtoMech 'significantly outperforms' PLT or faithfully recovers computation across tasks.

Steering gains are inconsistent across assays: for several DMS sets (e.g., GRB2_HUMAN_Faure_2021, RASK_HUMAN_Weng_2022_abundance) all methods, including ProtoMech, yield negative mean/top-k fitness scores, indicating the steering approach does not robustly generalize across functional landscapes despite being framed as broadly effective.

The reported phenomenon that ProtoMech circuits sometimes 'outperform' the original ESM2 model is presented as a beneficial 'denoising' effect, but this is in tension with the paper's central framing of CLTs as faithful replacement models that approximate ESM2's computation; an alternative, more concerning explanation (regularization artifacts unrelated to the original model's actual computation) is not ruled out.

Circuit discovery is anchored to supervised downstream probes (family classification, DMS fitness) rather than to the model's own pretraining objective (masked language modeling), which the authors acknowledge but justify only briefly; this leaves open whether the discovered circuits reflect general pLM computation or are artifacts of the specific supervised heads used to define the attribution targets.

Interpretation of circuits remains a manual, human-in-the-loop process cross-referencing UniProt/InterPro annotations, which the authors themselves list as a limitation restricting the scale and rigor of the qualitative validation and reproducibility of the specific biological claims.

strengths: Introduces a novel and timely extension of cross-layer transcoders (CLTs)—previously used for circuit tracing in LLMs—to protein language models (pLMs), addressing a genuine gap where prior SAE-based interpretability methods only factorize single-layer representations and cannot capture cross-layer computation.

Strong and consistent quantitative results: ProtoMech recovers 82-89% of full-model performance on protein family classification and function prediction while using <1% of the latent space, and consistently and substantially outperforms the natural per-layer transcoder (PLT) baseline across nearly all replacement-model variants and both model scales tested (ESM2-8M, ESM2-35M).

Thorough methodological rigor in the appendices: multiple replacement-model formulations (direct/sequential/full) are formalized and compared, extensive ablations are run (circuit discovery, latent counts per layer, stability of discovered circuits across seeds/folds, scaling to ESM2-35M, windowed CLTs for compute efficiency), which substantially strengthens confidence in the reported trends.

The steering application is a compelling and practically useful demonstration: circuit-based steering outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition and random mutation baselines on most DMS assays, and even outperforms dedicated black-box sequence optimizers (PEX, GGS) despite not being designed as an optimizer, suggesting the discovered circuits are actionable and not merely descriptive.

Qualitative case studies (kinase HRD motif/ATP-binding/glycine-rich loop, NADP+ binding Rossmann fold, GB1 mutation sensitivity) provide plausible, literature-grounded biological validation of the discovered circuits, and the associated interactive visualization tool is a valuable community resource that aids reproducibility and adoption.

The paper reports an interesting secondary finding (circuits occasionally outperforming the original model in low-performance regimes, attributed to a denoising effect), which is a thoughtful and non-obvious observation that adds scientific value beyond the main claims.
Code and visualizer are released; hyperparameters, training procedures, and dataset construction are documented in detail, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Biological validation of circuits is limited to a small number of hand-picked, qualitative case studies (three families/domains) rather than a systematic, large-scale, or statistically validated assessment of biological correspondence; the authors themselves note these are 'not exhaustive,' leaving open the possibility of selection bias in which examples are presented.

Experiments are restricted to relatively small pLMs (8M and 35M parameters), far below state-of-the-art production-scale pLMs (650M-15B parameters); the authors' own scaling table suggests full CLT training becomes prohibitively expensive at larger scales (e.g., ~10,000 GPU-days estimated for ESM2-15B), and while windowed CLTs are proposed as a mitigation, this is validated only on the 35M model with a single configuration, leaving practical scalability to real-world pLMs largely unresolved.

Steering gains, while favorable relative to baselines, are often modest or inconsistent in absolute terms across DMS assays (e.g., near-zero or negative mean scores for RASK_HUMAN and GRB2_HUMAN across all methods including ProtoMech), suggesting the method's practical utility for fitness improvement is assay-dependent rather than uniformly strong.

Circuit discovery relies on greedy, attribution-based latent selection, a heuristic known to be sensitive to correlated/superposed features; the sensitivity of discovered circuits to key hyperparameters (TopK sparsity k, auxiliary loss weight, latent dictionary size) is not systematically explored, leaving some uncertainty about how robust the reported circuits are to design choices.

The comparison to sparse autoencoder (SAE) approaches is largely conceptual/schematic (Appendix H) rather than a direct empirical head-to-head comparison on the same tasks, which would have better substantiated the claimed advantage of CLTs over decomposition-only methods.

Some headline claims (e.g., '71% of cases' where ProtoMech beats PLT in steering) aggregate across many settings without deeper analysis of effect-size distribution or statistical significance, making it harder to judge the practical magnitude of the reported advantages.
